Two-dimensional P-spline model

Source: R/model-psplines.R
p_splines.Rd

p_splines() smooths the log death rates over age and year with a Poisson P-spline surface and forecasts them by extending the surface over the forecast years (Currie, Durban and Eilers 2004). The code follows the reference implementation, Mort2Dsmooth() and predict.Mort2Dsmooth() of the R package MortalitySmooth 2.3.4 (Camarda), and reproduces its fitted values, forecasts and standard errors for given smoothing parameters.

Usage

p_splines(
  lambda = NULL,
  criterion = c("bic", "aic"),
  pord = 2,
  deg = 3,
  ndx = NULL,
  overdispersion = FALSE,
  lambda_range = c(1e-04, 1e+06),
  infant = FALSE
)

Arguments

lambda

Smoothing parameters over age and years, c(age, year); NULL (default) selects them by criterion.

criterion

"bic" (default) or "aic".

pord

Order of the difference penalties, over age and years (one value for both).

deg

Degree of the B-splines, over age and years.

ndx

Numbers of intervals between knots over age and years; NULL gives about one knot per five years (see Details).

overdispersion

FALSE (default): Poisson deaths. TRUE: one dispersion for all cells in the choice of the smoothing parameters and in the draws (MortalitySmooth). "age": a dispersion for each age that varies smoothly over age (Djeundje and Currie 2011; see Details).

lambda_range

Search range of the smoothing parameters (the default of MortalitySmooth). A selected value at an end of the range gives a warning (class mt_warning_lambda_bound) when the criterion improves by more than 1 two decades beyond it.

infant

Give the first year of life its own coefficients (Camarda 2019).

Value

A model specification.

Details

Model. The deaths of age x and year t are Poisson with mean E[x, t] m[x, t]. The log rates are a tensor-product B-spline surface, log m = Ba A t(By), with B-splines of degree deg on equally spaced knots over age (Ba) and over years (By) and a matrix of coefficients A. Differences of order pord between neighbouring coefficients are penalised, over age with weight lambda[1] and over years with weight lambda[2]. The coefficients maximise the penalised Poisson log-likelihood (penalised scoring algorithm, computed in array form). The smoothing parameters minimise the BIC (default) or the AIC, with the effective dimension (the trace of the hat matrix) as the number of parameters.

Forecast. The forecast is part of the fit. The basis over years is extended by B-splines on the same knot spacing beyond the last forecast year (and below the first year, as predict.Mort2Dsmooth() places the knots), and the forecast years enter with weight 0: they carry no data, and their coefficients follow from the penalty. With pord = 2 the coefficients continue about linearly, so each age continues the trend of its last years; the order of the penalty determines the form of the forecast. The model is fitted again on the extended basis with the smoothing parameters of the fit, as predict.Mort2Dsmooth() does. The penalty over age also acts on the added coefficients, so the fitted rates of the data years change slightly, and the forecast depends a little on the horizon through the last knot (up to 0.02 on the log scale for England and Wales men, ages 30-100, 10 years ahead).

Uncertainty. Draws come from the normal approximation of the coefficients, with the covariance (B'WB + P)^-1 of the penalised likelihood (W the fitted deaths, P the penalty). MortalitySmooth computes the standard errors of forecast log rates from this covariance. Over the forecast years the penalty acts as a prior: the variance grows with the horizon, the faster the smaller lambda[2]. Draws are paths of the whole surface, correlated over ages and years as in the model. They describe the expected rates; predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths. With overdispersion = TRUE, the dispersion psi2 (deviance divided by the number of cells minus the effective dimension) enters the choice of the smoothing parameters and the penalty, as in Mort2Dsmooth(overdispersion = TRUE), and the covariance is psi2 (B'WB + psi2 P)^-1. MortalitySmooth's predict() instead refits the forecast without psi2 in the penalty and multiplies the standard errors by sqrt(psi2).

Dispersion by age. overdispersion = "age" replaces the Poisson assumption by the first two moments of the deaths, E[D] = E m and var(D) = phi[x] E[D], with a dispersion phi[x] for each age that varies smoothly over age (Djeundje and Currie 2011, eq. 2.1; Model 3, eq. 5.26). Rates and dispersions are estimated by the bias corrected scheme of the paper (section 4):

  1. Start with phi = 1 at every age.

  2. Fit the rates by penalised quasi-likelihood: the scoring algorithm with the weights of the cells divided by their dispersion (eq. 3.13). The smoothing parameters minimise the criterion of the scaled deviance: the deviance of each cell divided by its dispersion, plus log(n) (BIC, eq. 3.16) or 2 (AIC) times the effective dimension.

  3. For each age, compute the bias-corrected mean Pearson statistic d[x]: the sum of (D - mu)^2 / mu over its years, divided by its number of cells n[x] minus its contribution to the effective dimension, the sum of its diagonal elements of the hat matrix (eq. 4.20 and 4.21).

  4. Smooth the statistics over age by penalised quasi-likelihood with E[d] = phi, var(d) = tau phi^2 / n[x] and the link -1 / phi = Ba beta (eq. 4.22): the B-splines over age of the rates and a difference penalty of order pord[1] (eq. 5.28). The smoothing parameter minimises the scaled BIC of this fit.

  5. Repeat steps 2 to 4 until no dispersion changes by more than 1e-5 relative to its value (section 5.2.2), at most 50 times.

The forecast fit keeps the dispersions of the ages in the weights, and the draws come from the covariance (B'WB + P)^-1 with W the fitted deaths divided by their dispersion. In the paper's example (CMI assured lives, ages 40-90, section 5.2.3) the dispersion down-weights the fit to the data and the selected surface is smoother: the effective dimension is 46 under the Poisson assumption, 36 with one dispersion and 33 with the dispersion by age, and the confidence intervals of the forecast are narrower. With a single age, "age" gives one dispersion, the bias-corrected mean Pearson statistic (eq. 4.20). The fit selects the smoothing parameters in every round, so it takes several times as long as the Poisson fit.

Data. Ages are placed at the midpoints of their cells, an open interval at its lower bound plus half the width of the interval below it (as in mt_smooth()). Cells with missing deaths or exposures, and cells without exposure, get weight 0, so the surface interpolates them. infant = TRUE gives the first year of life a row of coefficients of its own, penalised over years but not connected over age with the following ages (Camarda 2019, section 3.1); it applies when the grid starts with age group 0-1 and has at least four age groups.

Package-specific choices (reference unknown). By default the knots are about five years of age and five calendar years apart, floor(n / 5) intervals for n ages or years as in MortalitySmooth; for age groups wider than one year, n is the number of single years that the cell ages span. The smoothing parameters are searched on a grid with steps of 1 on the log10 scale, followed by a continuous search near the best grid point (MortalitySmooth: two grid searches with steps of 2 and 0.5). With overdispersion = "age": tau is the mean Pearson statistic of the smooth of step 4, sum(n[x] (d[x] - phi[x])^2 / phi[x]^2) divided by the number of ages minus its effective dimension, alternated with the choice of its smoothing parameter as psi2 with overdispersion = TRUE (at most 5 times; the paper estimates tau without stating how); that smoothing parameter is searched over lambda_range as those of the rates; ages without data get weight 0 in step 4, so the smooth gives their dispersion; predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths, as with overdispersion = TRUE, because the quasi-likelihood defines the mean and variance of the deaths but no distribution, and the paper gives no predictive distribution. The paper's full extended quasi-likelihood scheme (mean deviances by age, eq. 2.6) is not offered: it underestimates the dispersion (section 4, Figure 4), and the paper reports its results with the bias corrected scheme.

References

Currie ID, Durban M, Eilers PHC (2004). Smoothing and forecasting mortality rates. Statistical Modelling 4(4): 279-298. doi:10.1191/1471082X04st080oa

Camarda CG (2015). MortalitySmooth: Smoothing and forecasting Poisson counts with P-splines. R package version 2.3.4 (CRAN archive).

Camarda CG (2019). Smooth constrained mortality forecasting. Demographic Research 41(38): 1091-1130. doi:10.4054/DemRes.2019.41.38

Djeundje VAB, Currie ID (2011). Smoothing dispersed counts with applications to mortality data. Annals of Actuarial Science 5(1): 33-52. doi:10.1017/S1748499510000047

See also

cp_splines() for forecasts constrained to past age patterns and time trends; mt_smooth() for smoothing without forecasting.

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1995:2012)
fit <- mt_fit(p_splines(), x)
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 10, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
mt_parameters(fit)
#>     stratum   parameter  index        value
#>      <char>      <char> <char>        <num>
#>  1:  female  lambda_age        8.337861e-01
#>  2:  female lambda_year        1.206932e+04
#>  3:  female          ed        3.398214e+01
#>  4:  female         bic        1.804454e+03
#>  5:  female  dispersion        1.255109e+00
#>  6:    male  lambda_age        9.801742e-01
#>  7:    male lambda_year        3.600860e+03
#>  8:    male          ed        3.669204e+01
#>  9:    male         bic        1.575542e+03
#> 10:    male  dispersion        1.057821e+00
# dispersion that varies smoothly over age (Djeundje and Currie 2011),
# smoothing parameters of the rates given
fit_age <- mt_fit(p_splines(lambda = c(1, 1000), overdispersion = "age"), x)
p <- mt_parameters(fit_age)
p[parameter == "dispersion" & stratum == "female"]
